hints: Think about what the word monodentate means in terms of number, one tooth or one point of attachment to the central metal.
walkthrough:
Break down the word monodentate**
Picture mono as one and dentate as tooth. A monodentate ligand bites the metal only once, so it can only attach at one point.

Link to bonding**
A ligand bonds by donating a lone pair into an empty orbital on the metal. Since there is only one attachment point, it donates one lone pair and forms one dative covalent bond to the metal atom or ion.
Final answer: A ligand that donates one lone pair to form one dative bond to the central metal atom or ion.

hints: Recall that octahedral means coordination number 6, so work out how many monodentate CO or CN- ligands fit around one Mo or Fe3+.
Add up charges to find the overall complex charge, remembering CO is neutral while CN- is 1- and Fe is 3+.
walkthrough:
Use octahedral to get the number of ligands**
Octahedral always means six positions around the central metal. Both CO and $\text{CN}^-$ are monodentate, so one ligand occupies one position. You need six of each: $\text{Mo(CO)}_6$ and $\text{Fe(CN)}_6$.

Add charges carefully**
For molybdenum, Mo is present as an atom (oxidation state 0) and CO is neutral, so $0 + 6(0) = 0$. The complex is neutral. For iron, $\text{Fe}^{3+} + 6 \times (1-) = 3+ + 6- = 3-$. So the ion is $\text{[Fe(CN)}_6\text{]}^{3-}$.

Final answer: Molybdenum complex: formula $\text{Mo(CO)}_6$, charge 0 (neutral).
Iron(III) complex: formula $\text{Fe(CN)}_6$, charge $3-$, i.e. $\text{[Fe(CN)}_6\text{]}^{3-}$.

hints: Visualise an octahedral Fe centre with six CN groups, four in a plane and one above and one below, and think which pair are directly opposite each other.
walkthrough:
Sketch octahedral in 3D**
Put Fe in the centre. Draw four $\text{CN}$ groups in a square plane around it, using a solid wedge for the bond coming out toward you and a hashed wedge for the bond going back. Then draw one $\text{CN}$ straight up and one straight down.

Label the trans angle**
Any two ligands directly opposite each other through Fe, for example the top and bottom $\text{CN}$ groups, are at $180^{\circ}$. Mark that angle clearly on your diagram.

Final answer: 3D octahedral diagram centred on Fe with six $\text{CN}^-$ ligands (four in plane with wedge and hashed wedge, one up, one down) and a $180^{\circ}$ angle labelled between any trans pair.

hints: Start from the blue aqueous ion $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ and count how many waters must be replaced to give $\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$.
walkthrough:
Identify starting and finishing complexes**
In dilute copper(II) sulfate the copper exists as $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$. Excess $\text{NH}_3$ replaces four of the six waters, leaving two waters in the product $\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$.

Balance ligands and charge**
Four $\text{NH}_3$ go in, four $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ come out. Charge stays $2+$ on both sides, and sulfate is a spectator so it is omitted in the ionic equation: $$\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Remember that in an isolated ion the five d-orbitals have the same energy, but approaching ligands change this.
Think about what a partially filled d-shell allows an electron to do when white light shines on the complex.
Connect the energy gap between split d-orbitals to absorption of a specific photon of light.
Recall that the colour you see is not the colour absorbed but the rest of the white light that is left over.
walkthrough:
Split the d-orbitals**
On its own $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ has five degenerate d-orbitals. When ligands approach, they repel d-electrons unequally, so the set splits into lower and higher energy levels separated by $\Delta E$.

Promote an electron with light**
$\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is $3d^9$, so there is a vacancy in the upper set. An electron in a lower d-orbital can absorb exactly $\Delta E$ from a photon of visible light and jump up. This is a d-d transition.

Absorb one colour, see the opposite**
Only the wavelength whose photon energy equals $\Delta E$ is absorbed. All other wavelengths pass through or are reflected. Your eye sees the mixture left over, which is the complementary colour to that absorbed. That is why copper(II) complexes look blue.

Put the story together**
Splitting provides the gap, light provides the energy to jump the gap, absorption removes one colour, and the complement is observed. No splitting or no partial d-shell would mean no colour in this way.

Final answer: Ligands cause the d-orbitals to split into two sets of different energy.
An electron absorbs a photon of light ( $h\nu$ ) and is promoted from a lower to a higher d-orbital.
The colour observed is the complement of the colour absorbed, the remaining light transmitted or reflected.

hints: Identify the new ligand supplied by concentrated HCl and the likely formula of Z, $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$, and think what happens to coordinated NH3 in strong acid.
Balance Cu, Cl, N and H by forming $\text{NH}_4^+$ from $\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+$ and releasing the two remaining waters.
walkthrough:
Spot the product Z**
Concentrated $\text{HCl}$ provides a huge excess of $\text{Cl}^-$, which replaces all $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands to give the tetrachlorocuprate(II) ion, $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$. In acid, the displaced $\text{NH}_3$ is protonated to $\text{NH}_4^+$.

Balance the full equation**
You need $4\text{HCl}$ to supply $4\text{Cl}^-$ for Z and $4\text{H}^+$ to make $4\text{NH}_4^+$. The two waters are simply released: $$\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CuCl}_4^{2-} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 4\text{NH}_4^+$$ Check charge: $2+ = 2- + 4(+1) = 2+$, and atoms balance.
Final answer: $\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CuCl}_4^{2-} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 4\text{NH}_4^+$ (Z is $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$)

hints: Focus on what is happening to the ligands around Cu when NH3 and H2O are swapped for Cl-, the metal oxidation state does not change.
walkthrough:
Name the swap**
The copper stays as $\text{Cu(II)}$, only the groups attached to it change. $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ leave and $\text{Cl}^-$ enters. That direct swap of ligands is called ligand exchange, also accepted as ligand substitution, replacement or displacement.
Final answer: Ligand exchange (substitution / replacement / displacement).

hints: Count the ligands in $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$ and recall the shape adopted by four large chloride ligands around Cu(II).
walkthrough:
Count to four**
Z is $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$ with coordination number 4. With four bulky $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands, the complex arranges to minimise repulsion in a tetrahedral geometry with bond angles near $109.5^{\circ}$.
Final answer: Tetrahedral.

hints: Recall the classic colour change from dark blue ammine complex to the chloride complex in concentrated HCl.
walkthrough:
Remember the classic observation**
Adding excess concentrated $\text{HCl}$ to the dark blue $\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$ gives a yellow solution of $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$. This blue to yellow change is a standard test for this ligand exchange.
Final answer: Yellow (yellow-green solution).

hints: Think about what controls the size of the d-orbital energy gap when you change the ligand from NH3 and H2O to Cl- and change octahedral to tetrahedral.
walkthrough:
Link ligand to energy gap**
Colour comes from $\Delta E$ between split d-orbitals. $\text{Cl}^-$ is a different ligand from $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and the geometry also changes from octahedral to tetrahedral, so the extent of splitting changes. A different $\Delta E$ means a different frequency and colour of light is absorbed, so a different complementary colour is seen.
Final answer: Different ligands cause different d-orbital splitting, so $\Delta E$ changes and a different wavelength of light is absorbed.
